subject: chemistry
title: The Three Realms of Matter
welcome_lead: Step into a world where everything you see is made of tiny particles arranged in three different ways.
meta_desc: Explore solids, liquids and gases in this KS3 chemistry adventure on the three states of matter.
final_note: You now know how particles arrange themselves in solids, liquids and gases.

concepts.def: Particles packed in a fixed regular pattern, only vibrating.
Particles close together but able to slide past each other.
Particles far apart and moving quickly in all directions.
A property of solids: they keep their own shape.
Solids and liquids keep the same volume.
Gases can be squashed because particles are spread out.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Everything around you is made of particles. The way these particles are arranged and how they move decides whether something is a solid, a liquid or a gas.

Same particles, different arrangements.

In a solid, particles are packed tightly in a regular pattern. They cannot move around, they only vibrate on the spot.

That is why a solid has a fixed shape and fixed volume.

In a liquid, particles are still close together but can slide around. Liquids take the shape of their container but keep a fixed volume.

In a gas, particles are far apart and zoom around quickly. Gases fill any container and can be compressed.

mcqs.q: Why is the hydration enthalpy of a small, highly charged ion very exothermic?
options: Hydration enthalpy only depends on the size of the ion, not its charge.
Kc is always dimensionless.
Small/highly charged ions form strong ion-dipole attractions with water molecules, releasing a large amount of energy.
Hydration enthalpy is the same for all ions because water molecules are identical.

mcqs.q: What are the units of Kc for a reaction?
options: Kc is always dimensionless.
A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.
Kc always has units of mol dm^-3.
They depend on Δn (the difference between moles of gaseous/aqueous products and reactants) — Kc can be dimensionless or have units like mol dm^-3.

mcqs.q: How is a dynamic equilibrium different from a static one?
options: Kc is always dimensionless.
Dynamic and static equilibria are the same thing because both show constant macroscopic properties.
A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.
In a dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; in a static equilibrium, nothing is happening at the particle level.

free_texts.q: What is the name of the state where particles vibrate in a fixed pattern? (one word)

sequence.def: Particles vibrate in fixed positions — below 0°C
At 0°C ice turns to liquid water
Particles move around each other — between 0 and 100°C
At 100°C water turns rapidly to gas
Gas particles spread out and move fast — above 100°C
